items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the distance of open water over which the wind blows to generate waves”.

items.stem: Explain how waves are formed.
items.answer: Friction between wind and the sea surface transfers energy, forming ripples that grow into waves; size depends on wind speed, duration and fetch; water particles move in orbits, so energy rather than water travels forward.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Explain the process of wave refraction and its effect on a coastline of headlands and bays.
items.answer: Waves slow in shallow water off headlands so crests bend to become parallel with the coast; energy converges on headlands (erosion) and diverges in bays (deposition); the coast is gradually straightened.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed point [4]

items.stem: Compare constructive and destructive waves.
items.answer: Constructive: low height, long wavelength, low frequency (6-8 per minute), spilling breakers, swash stronger than backwash, build berms. Destructive: high, steep, frequent (10-14 per minute), plunging breakers, strong backwash, remove material and steepen then flatten beaches.

items.stem: Explain the processes of marine erosion.

items.stem: Explain the concept of a sediment cell.
items.answer: A closed system with sources (cliff erosion, rivers, offshore), transfers (longshore drift) and sinks (beaches, spits, offshore); boundaries at headlands; interference in one part affects others down-drift.

items.stem: “The sediment cell is the most useful concept for understanding coastal processes.” How far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: It links erosion, transport and deposition as one system with inputs, stores and outputs, explains down-drift effects and underpins shoreline management plans. Against: Boundaries are leaky; it says little about rates of erosion of particular cliffs, which depend on geology, wave energy and sub-aerial processes; sea-level change alters cells. Conclusion: The concept is a powerful framework, especially for management, but must be combined with an understanding of local processes.

items.stem: Explain why groynes at one place can cause erosion further along the coast.
items.answer: They trap sediment moving by longshore drift; less sediment reaches down-drift beaches, which become narrower and offer less protection, so cliffs behind erode faster (e.g. Mappleton, Holderness).

items.stem: Explain how sub-aerial processes contribute to cliff retreat.
items.answer: Weathering (freeze-thaw, wetting and drying, biological, solution) weakens rock; rainfall saturates clays, raising pore pressure and causing slumps, slides and falls; the debris is removed by waves, exposing fresh rock.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [4]

items.stem: Explain the difference between eustatic and isostatic sea-level change.
items.answer: Eustatic change is global, caused by changes in ocean water volume (ice melting and growth, thermal expansion); isostatic change is local, caused by vertical movement of the land (loading by ice, sediment, rebound).

items.stem: “Marine processes are more important than sub-aerial processes in the retreat of cliffs.” How far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Waves undercut cliffs by hydraulic action and abrasion and remove debris; without removal, cliffs would stabilise. Against: On weak clay cliffs, rain-induced slumping supplies most retreat; weathering weakens chalk and limestone; relative importance varies with rock type, climate and exposure. Conclusion: Marine processes control the long-term rate by removing debris, but sub-aerial processes are often the immediate cause of retreat on weak cliffs.

items.stem: Explain why parts of Scotland are rising while south-east England is sinking.
items.answer: Scotland is still rebounding after the removal of the ice sheet; south-east England, beyond the ice margin, is subsiding as the crust readjusts (a see-saw effect), as well as compaction of sediments.

items.answer: (a) Plunging breakers with a strong backwash drag sediment offshore, forming offshore bars; the beach is lowered and a storm ridge may form at the top; the profile is flattened. Outputs: longshore drift out of the cell 402, offshore transport 267, dredging and extraction 67. (a) Suggest the likely effect on the budget of protecting the cliffs with a sea wall. (b) Explain how sediment is transported along the coast.
items.answer: (a) Inputs fall by up to 290 thousand m³, so the budget would become −374 thousand m³ per year; beaches down-drift would be starved of sediment. (b) Longshore drift: swash moves material up the beach at the angle of approach of the waves, backwash returns it at right angles under gravity, giving a zigzag movement; also traction, saltation, suspension and solution.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “sub-aerial processes”?
options: A local change in the level of the land relative to the sea, for example rebound after ice sheets melt.
A global change in sea level caused by a change in the volume of water in the oceans.
Weathering and mass movement acting on the land surface of a coast, above the reach of the sea.
A mass movement in which saturated material slides along a curved slip plane.
items.answer: Weathering and mass movement acting on the land surface of a coast, above the reach of the sea.
items.markingKey: Sub-aerial processes: weathering and mass movement acting on the land surface of a coast, above the reach of the sea. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Cliffs of weak rock can retreat by over a metre a year.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Holderness boulder clay cliffs retreat at about 1.8 m a year on average.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Sea level rise is the same everywhere on Earth.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why parts of Scotland are rising while south-east England is sinking.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Relative sea-level change varies with land movement, ocean currents and gravity effects. (b) Scotland is still rebounding after the removal of the ice sheet; south-east England, beyond the ice margin, is subsiding as the crust readjusts (a see-saw effect), as well as compaction of sediments.

items.stem: Fig. 5.3 shows the total distance the cliff top at Happisburgh, Norfolk (glacial sands and clays) had retreated from its 2000 position: 2000: 0 m, 2005: 8 m, 2010: 23 m, 2015: 30 m, 2020: 36.9 m. items.answer: Rising sea level and more intense storms allow waves to reach the cliff foot more often; wetter winters increase slumping; defences up-drift reduce beach protection.

items.answer: Destructive wave

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how waves are formed. (b) A revision website states: “Destructive waves always make beaches steeper.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Friction between wind and the sea surface transfers energy, forming ripples that grow into waves; size depends on wind speed, duration and fetch; water particles move in orbits, so energy rather than water travels forward. (b) Not correct. They often comb material offshore, lowering the beach gradient.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the process of wave refraction and its effect on a coastline of headlands and bays. (b) Compare constructive and destructive waves.
items.answer: (a) Waves slow in shallow water off headlands so crests bend to become parallel with the coast; energy converges on headlands (erosion) and diverges in bays (deposition); the coast is gradually straightened. (b) Constructive: low height, long wavelength, low frequency (6-8 per minute), spilling breakers, swash stronger than backwash, build berms. Destructive: high, steep, frequent (10-14 per minute), plunging breakers, strong backwash, remove material and steepen then flatten beaches.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per developed point [4] (b) 1 mark per comparison [4]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a stretch of coast, often bounded by headlands, within which sediment movement is largely self-contained”.
items.answer: Sediment cell

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why groynes at one place can cause erosion further along the coast. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Most beach sediment on some coasts comes from rivers.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) They trap sediment moving by longshore drift; less sediment reaches down-drift beaches, which become narrower and offer less protection, so cliffs behind erode faster (e.g. Mappleton, Holderness). (b) Correct. Rivers supply much sediment on many coasts, though dams can reduce this supply.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Sediment cells are completely closed systems.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the concept of a sediment cell.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Fine sediment and material in storms can move between cells. (b) A closed system with sources (cliff erosion, rivers, offshore), transfers (longshore drift) and sinks (beaches, spits, offshore); boundaries at headlands; interference in one part affects others down-drift.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [3]
